paras: The expulsion of a Black man from Lewistown was an incident in the summer of 1880 or earlier in which an unnamed "colored man" was pelted with rotten eggs and driven out of town after being accused of insulting a white woman on the street. It is known only through an exchange between two newspaper editors over whether the act resembled the expulsions of Black people in the South.

The surviving account gives no date, no name for the man and no description of those who attacked him. According to the Juniata Sentinel and Republican of Mifflintown, the man was "rotten-egged out of town for insulting a white woman on the street." The Sentinel's account indicates that the incident occurred no later than about mid-July 1880, since the editor of the Selinsgrove Times had been commenting on it "during the past two weeks" before the Sentinel's issue of 4 August.
No report of an arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage, nor of where the man went.

The Selinsgrove Times, edited by a man the Sentinel called Weirick, objected to the expulsion, and according to the Sentinel it put the rotten-egging "upon the same level" as driving a colored man out of a community in the South. The Times' own articles were not found, so its position is known only as its opponent described it.

The Sentinel answered on 4 August that "there is no similarity in the cases," arguing that the man "had no right to insult a lady on the street" and that the offense touched "every decent man in the community." It held that Black people in the South were driven out "because of opinion's sake," not for insults to women, and called the Lewistown man "dangerous to society generally," with opinions "of the most pernicious quality." Turning the comparison around, the editorial likened the expelled man to the Southern "bull dozer," since in its view both kept others from exercising their rights.
No coverage of the incident in the Black press was found, and the Sentinel's editorial is the only surviving report.

reader.title: Expulsion of a Black man from Lewistown (1880)
bases: A1 says the man was "rotten-egged out of town" and "driven out of Lewistown"; no killing or threat to kill is reported.
The only report is the Sentinel's secondhand editorial account (A1), which itself relies on the Selinsgrove Times' comments; no Times text, local report or Black-press coverage was found.

accounts.label: Juniata Sentinel editorial (relaying the Selinsgrove Times)
accounts.gist: A colored man in Lewistown was rotten-egged out of town for insulting a white woman on the street; the Sentinel holds that he deserved it and that the case differs from Southern expulsions.

framing.detail: The Sentinel argued "there is no similarity in the cases" with Southern expulsions, said the man "had no right to insult a lady on the street," and called his opinions "of the most pernicious quality."

As characterized by the Sentinel, the Selinsgrove Times expressed "unhappiness" over the rotten-egging and put it "upon the same level" as driving a colored man out of a Southern community; the Times' own text was not found.

record_check.dossier: Undated in the text; only bounded as before about 20 July 1880 (the Times had been commenting for two weeks before 4 August); it could be earlier than July.
The text says only "Lewistown"; Pennsylvania (and so Mifflin County) is inferred from the reporting paper's Mifflintown, Pa. masthead, not stated.

record_check.record: according to the Selinsgrove Times as cited in an editorial
record_check.dossier: Correct: the Juniata Sentinel's editorial relays the incident from the Times' criticism of it and defends the expulsion.
Supported; the man was also pelted with rotten eggs.
